tests.description: Timed check on Augustus & the Principate

questions.question: Q: How did Octavian become Augustus?
questions.correctAnswer: After Caesar's assassination (44 BC), Octavian joined the Second Triumvirate with Antony and Lepidus. After defeating Caesar's assassins, the Triumvirate collapsed. Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BC). In 27 BC the Senate granted him the title Augustus (revered one), and he established the Principate, maintaining Republican forms while holding supreme power.

questions.question: Q: What was the constitutional settlement of 27 BC?
questions.correctAnswer: Augustus formally 'returned' power to the Senate and people, who then granted him consulship, tribunician power and control of provinces with armies (Gaul, Spain, Syria, Egypt). This gave him command of the army while appearing to restore the Republic. The arrangement was renewed in 23 BC with tribunician power as his primary authority.

questions.question: Q: How did Augustus maintain the illusion of the Republic?
questions.correctAnswer: He refused the title of king or dictator, used the title Princeps (First Citizen), held traditional Republican offices (consul, tribune), consulted the Senate, held elections, and allowed the Senate to govern 'senatorial' provinces. The reality was that he controlled the army, the treasury and the key provinces, making him effectively a monarch.

questions.question: Q: What were Augustus' main reforms?
questions.correctAnswer: Military: standing army of 28 legions with fixed terms of service and a praetorian guard. Moral: laws promoting marriage, discouraging adultery and encouraging childbearing. Religious: revived traditional cults and temples. Building: massive construction programme (forums, temples, theatres). Administrative: reformed taxation and provincial government.

questions.question: Q: What was the Pax Romana and why was it significant?
questions.correctAnswer: The Pax Romana was a period of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire lasting about 200 years from Augustus. It enabled trade, cultural exchange, road building and economic prosperity throughout the Mediterranean world. It represented Augustus' greatest legacy: the end of civil wars and the beginning of stable imperial government.
